paras: The hazing of the Cortney brothers was an attack in late April or early May 1919 in which white students at the University of Maine in Orono covered two Black sophomores, Roger and Daniel (or Samuel) Cortney, with molasses and feathers. Black newspapers reported it as the tarring and feathering of 'Negro students' by a mob, while the university's president issued a statement denying that race was the cause.

The brothers were sophomores who, according to the Chicago Defender, had been 'exceedingly popular' and members of the glee and musical clubs. The Baltimore Afro-American called them Roger and Samuel Courney, sons of a Boston physician, while the New York World special reprinted in Black weeklies said their names were kept secret. Accounts of what led up to the attack differ, but the Afro-American and the Defender both describe a clash in which three white students ended up unconscious or on the floor.

According to the Defender, freshmen gathered at the brothers' room as 'agents for the awaiting throng' outside, and after the scuffle the two escaped by the back entrance. The World special said eighty white students invaded their rooms and that the two climbed down a rope ladder and ran to Old Town, several miles away, 'pursued by a yelling mob'.

Freshmen split into three groups to search Orono and Oldtown and found the brothers at Oldtown, the Defender reported. In the World's version, halters were put around their necks and they were led back toward the campus, where tar and feathers had been prepared and bystanders tried in vain to dissuade the students. The Defender described a 'great ring' of students on the campus in which the brothers were allowed to tell their side and then made to pour two jugs of molasses over each other before feathers were thrown on them.

President R. J. Aley of the University of Maine issued a formal statement saying that 'Colored students' were welcome and well treated and that the faculty did not condone the affair, which it called extremely regrettable. He added that such an affair was likely to happen at any college, its gravity depending on 'the susceptibilities of the victim and the notoriety given it'. The World special claimed that school and State authorities were trying to keep the affair quiet, and no report of arrests or of discipline of the white students appears in the coverage.

The Afro-American broke the story on May 9 with a short Bangor item headed 'MOLASSED AND FEATHERED' that presented the attack as retaliation for the brothers' knocking out three white students. On May 17 the Philadelphia Tribune ran the World special on its front page as 'COLORED STUDENTS TARRED AND FEATURED IN MAINE', and Cayton's Weekly in Seattle carried the same text in its 'Did You Know That' column a week later. The Chicago Defender gave the fullest narrative on its May 24 front page, naming the brothers and stressing their resistance and their standing at school.

The Associated Negro Press then circulated the president's denial, which the St. Louis Argus headed 'NO RACE TROUBLE AT UNIVERSITY OF MAINE', the Omaha Monitor 'HAZING NOT DUE TO THE COLOR QUESTION' and the Savannah Tribune 'RACE QUESTION NOT THE CAUSE'. The Cleveland Advocate printed the same statement under 'University President Defends Student Hazing' inside a front-page column on newspapers demanding an end to lynching.

The cause is told four ways: the Afro-American said the brothers had knocked out three white students who planned to haze them, reportedly with clubs, while the president said the freshmen were repaying 'treatment' received from the two sophomores. The World special said instead that the two had been expelled before the students came for them, a claim no other report repeats. The accounts also differ on the capture, which the World and the Defender describe as a pursuit to Old Town but the president's statement describes as the sophomores giving themselves up.
Only the World special mentions tar and halters; the Afro-American, the Defender and the president all speak of molasses and feathers.

reader.title: Hazing of the Cortney brothers at the University of Maine
bases: A crowd of white students pursued, seized and covered two Black students with molasses (or tar) and feathers; no killing or threat to kill is reported [A5, A8, A1].

The Afro-American's Bangor dispatch, the Defender, the World special and the president's statement independently agree that two sophomore brothers were covered with molasses or tar and feathers by students [A1, A5, A8, A3].

accounts.label: Bangor dispatch
accounts.gist: The brothers knocked unconscious three white students who planned to haze them, reportedly with clubs, and were then covered with molasses and feathers.

accounts.label: New York World special
accounts.gist: After the two had been expelled, eighty white students invaded their rooms; they fled by rope ladder to Old Town, were caught, haltered, led back near the campus and tarred and feathered, while authorities tried to keep it quiet.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender
accounts.gist: The brothers resisted freshmen acting for a crowd outside their room, leaving three freshmen on the floor, and escaped; freshmen in three groups found them at Oldtown, ringed them on campus and made them pour molasses on each other before throwing feathers.

accounts.label: University president
accounts.gist: Freshmen resenting treatment from the two sophomores visited their room; after a scuffle the sophomores escaped but later gave themselves up and were hazed with molasses and feathers; race was not the cause.

framing.detail: The Philadelphia Tribune ran it on the front page as 'COLORED STUDENTS TARRED AND FEATURED IN MAINE', stressing the 'yelling mob', halters and official secrecy.
The Afro-American's brief 'MOLASSED AND FEATHERED' gave the attack as retaliation for the brothers knocking out three white students.
The Defender told the brothers' resistance and capture in detail and stressed that they had been 'exceedingly popular' at school.
ANP papers printed the president's denial under headlines such as 'NO RACE TROUBLE AT UNIVERSITY OF MAINE' and 'HAZING NOT DUE TO THE COLOR QUESTION' without comment.
The Cleveland Advocate headed the same statement 'University President Defends Student Hazing' and set it within a column on editorials demanding an end to lynching.

Roger and Daniel Cortney in the Defender; Roger and Samuel Courney in the Afro-American.
Knocking out three white students who planned to haze them (Afro-American); 'treatment' of freshmen (president).

info: Late April or the first days of May 1919: a Bangor dispatch dated May 7 placed it 'last week'; later reports carry datelines of May 12 and after.
University of Maine campus, Orono, Maine; the brothers were caught at Old Town (Oldtown), several miles away, and brought back to the campus.

Two brothers, Black students and sophomores at the University of Maine: Roger and Daniel Cortney (Defender) or Roger and Samuel Courney, sons of a Boston physician (Afro-American); the World special said their names were kept secret.

Versions differ: knocking unconscious three white students who planned to haze them, reportedly with clubs (Afro-American); three freshmen found lying on the floor of their room (Defender); 'treatment' the freshmen had received from them (university president).
White students of the University of Maine, described as freshmen (Defender, president's statement) and as eighty white students and 'a yelling mob' (World special).
The World special said the two had been expelled before the attack; no other report of discipline of either side was found.

sources.note: Earliest report (Bangor, May 7, 'MOLASSED AND FEATHERED'): Roger and Samuel Courney, sons of a Boston physician, molassed and feathered 'last week' for knocking out three white students who planned to haze them.
quotes: Roger and Samuel Courney, sons of a Boston physician were covered with molasses and feathers at the University of Maine last week for knocking unconscious three white students

sources.note: Front page, heavily garbled OCR (dateline Bangor, May 12): two unnamed Negro students from Boston, eighty white students, rope ladder, flight to Old Town, tar and feathers; same text as A8.
quotes: COLORED STUDENTS TARRED AND FEATURED IN MAINE

sources.note: Continuation ('Cortneys Captured', 'Popular at School'): freshmen in three groups found the brothers at Oldtown; ring on campus; forced to pour two jugs of molasses on each other; feathers; both sophomores in the glee and musical clubs.
quotes: two jugs of molasses were prepared and the brothers were forced to empty the contents upon each other. Feathers were then thrown upon them.
